items.title: Acemoglu and Robinson argue institutions explain development
items.claim: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson's 2001 AER paper used settler mortality as an instrument for institutional quality. What did they find?

options.text: Places where European settlement was deadly (tropics) developed 'extractive' colonial institutions; places suitable for settlement got 'inclusive' institutions. Institutional differences persist and explain a large share of cross-country income variation today

items.reveal:
The 2001 AER paper used settler mortality data to instrument for current institutions (since geography affects mortality but, AJR argue, only affects current outcomes through institutions). Their book 'Why Nations Fail' (2012) developed the inclusive vs extractive institutions framework for a general audience.

Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson won the 2024 Nobel for this body of work. Critics (Glaeser, Sachs) have argued for the role of geography, human capital and culture; the debate over weights between institutional and other factors continues.
items.why: Cross-country growth differences are large and persistent. Identifying causal drivers is genuinely difficult; AJR's instrumental approach was an influential attempt.

items.title: Tulip mania was less extreme than the legend
items.claim: Charles Mackay's 1841 'Extraordinary Popular Delusions' painted 17th-century Dutch tulip mania as a society-wide frenzy that crashed the economy. What does modern research find?

options.text: The crash bankrupted the Dutch Republic for a generation

Trading was confined largely to a small group of professional florists meeting in taverns; while bulb prices rose sharply and crashed in February 1637, the macro impact was modest and Mackay's tales of devastated cobblers are mostly unverified
Tulip mania never happened; it is a complete fabrication
It triggered the Eighty Years' War

items.reveal_title: A bubble, but a smaller one
items.reveal:
Anne Goldgar's 'Tulipmania' (2007) used archival records to show that bulb trading was largely among well-off merchants, that few contracts were ever actually enforced after the February 1637 crash, and that contemporary Calvinist moral pamphlets exaggerated the social ruin for didactic purposes.

Peter Garber argued similarly from an economist's perspective: peak prices for rare bulbs may have reflected genuine scarcity and fashion premiums, not pure delusion.

Mackay's account was readable, lurid and influential — but not historical.
items.why: Pop economic history is full of morality tales. The actual record is usually messier and less satisfying — but it's what students of bubbles need to grapple with.

items.title: Carbon pricing is the textbook fix for a textbook problem
items.claim: Climate change is often described as the largest market failure ever (Stern Review 2006). What's the standard economic prescription?

options.text: Pigouvian carbon pricing (tax or cap-and-trade) to internalise the social cost of carbon emissions; complementary policies for innovation, transition support and distributional fairness

items.reveal:
Arthur Pigou's 'Economics of Welfare' (1920) introduced taxes to internalise externalities. William Nordhaus's DICE model (1990s onwards) extended welfare economics to climate; he won the 2018 Nobel.

Real-world implementation: EU ETS (2005, world's largest cap-and-trade); UK Carbon Price Floor; Canada's federal carbon tax; California; Korea. Coverage and prices vary widely. As of 2023, ~25% of global emissions had a carbon price; average price below social cost estimates.

Distributional concerns and political economy of carbon pricing have limited adoption despite theoretical consensus.
items.why: Welfare economics provides a clear policy answer to climate change. Implementation is constrained by political economy more than by economic theory.
